case_studies.title: Automated Customization of LLMs for Enterprise Code Repositories Using Semantic Scopes
case_studies.abstract: Code completion (CC) is a task frequently used by developers when working in collaboration with LLM-based programming assistants. Despite the increased performance of LLMs on public benchmarks, out of the box LLMs still have a hard time generating code that aligns with a private code repository not previously seen by the model's training data. Customizing code LLMs to a private repository provides a way to improve the model performance. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models (LLMs) struggling to generate code that aligns with a private code repository. The authors built a system to automate the customization of LLMs for enterprise code repositories using semantic scopes. The result is improved model performance on private repositories.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage code repositories, here is what to do: review your current LLM-based programming assistants, consider implementing automated customization using semantic scopes, and evaluate the performance improvement on your private repositories.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper shows potential for improving LLM performance in enterprise settings, with real industry case studies. While the concepts aren't new, the approach to automated customization is valuable and actionable for IT engineers.

To address this, we explore effective and scalable methods for a hallucination detection in LLM-generated code review comments without the reference. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of Large Language Models generating ungrounded code review comments, by building a system called HalluJudge that detects hallucinations in automated code review comments. HalluJudge assesses the grounding of generated review comments based on context alignment. The result is a more reliable code review automation process.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage code review automation using Large Language Models, here is what to do: step 1, assess your current model's hallucination risk, step 2, consider integrating HalluJudge or similar detection methods, step 3, monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of the detection method in your workflow.

case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of correlating and responding to security alerts in Security Operations Centers by building a multi-layered AI framework called AgentSOC, which resulted in improved automation of security operations. case_studies.title: Beyond LLM-based test automation: A Zero-Cost Self-Healing Approach Using DOM Accessibility Tree Extraction
case_studies.abstract: Modern web test automation frameworks rely heavily on CSS selectors, XPath expressions, and visible text labels to locate UI elements. These locators are inherently brittle -- when web applications update their DOM structure or class names, test suites fail at scale. Existing self-healing approaches increasingly delegate element discovery to Large Language Models (LLMs), introducing per-run API costs that become prohibitive at enterprise scale. This paper presents a zero-cost self-healing test automation framework that replaces LLM-based discovery with a structured accessibility tree extractio
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of brittle test automation locators by building a zero-cost self-healing framework that uses DOM accessibility tree extraction, resulting in more reliable test suites. The framework replaces Large Language Model-based discovery, reducing costs. This is relevant to managing cloud infrastructure that supports web test automation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage web test automation frameworks, here is what to do: review your current locator strategies, consider implementing DOM accessibility tree extraction, and assess the potential cost savings from reduced Large Language Model API costs. This flags a risk: if your org uses LLM-based test automation, check your API costs immediately.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel approach to self-healing test automation, potentially applicable in real-world settings, leveraging accessibility tree extraction without relying on expensive LLM APIs.

case_studies.abstract: Modern web dashboards and enterprise applications increasingly rely on complex, distributed microservices architectures. While these architectures offer scalability, they introduce significant challenges in debugging and observability. When failures occur, they often manifest as opaque error messages to the end-user such as Something went wrong. This masks the underlying root cause which may reside in browser side exceptions, API contract violations, or server side logic failures. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of debugging complex web dashboards by building a system that automatically identifies and explains errors in plain language. The result is a more efficient and effective way to identify and fix issues in distributed microservices architectures. This research aims to provide more informative error messages to end-users and developers.

case_studies.title: GPA: Learning GUI Process Automation from Demonstrations
case_studies.abstract: GUI Process Automation (GPA) is a lightweight but general vision-based Robotic Process Automation (RPA), which enables fast and stable process replay with only a single demo. Addressing the fragility of traditional RPA and the non-deterministic risks of current vision language model-based GUI agents, GPA introduces three core benefits: (1) Robustness via Sequential Monte Carlo-based localization to handle rescaling and detection uncertainty; (2) Deterministic and Reliability safeguarded by readiness calibration; and (3) Privacy through fast, fully local execution. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of fragile and unreliable Robotic Process Automation (RPA) by introducing a lightweight and general vision-based approach called GUI Process Automation (GPA). The researchers built a system that can learn GUI automation from demonstrations and achieve fast and stable process replay. The result is a more robust and reliable automation solution.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage automated workflows or RPA systems, here is what to do: review your current RPA solutions for fragility and reliability issues, consider GPA as a potential replacement or upgrade, and evaluate its benefits for your organization's specific use case.

case_studies.title: Terminal Agents Suffice for Enterprise Automation
case_studies.abstract: There has been growing interest in building agents that can interact with digital platforms to execute meaningful enterprise tasks autonomously. Among the approaches explored are tool-augmented agents built on abstractions such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) and web agents that operate through graphical interfaces. Yet, it remains unclear whether such complex agentic systems are necessary given their cost and operational overhead. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of automating enterprise tasks by showing that simple terminal-based agents can be effective, the authors built a coding agent that interacts directly with platforms, and the result is a more efficient and cost-effective solution. The agent can execute tasks autonomously without needing complex systems. This research aims to simplify enterprise automation.

case_studies.title: Automating Domain-Driven Design: Experience with a Prompting Framework
case_studies.abstract: Domain-driven design (DDD) is a powerful design technique for architecting complex software systems. This paper introduces a prompting framework that automates core DDD activities through structured large language model (LLM) interactions. We decompose DDD into five sequential steps: (1) establishing an ubiquitous language, (2) simulating event storming, (3) identifying bounded contexts, (4) designing aggregates, and (5) mapping to technical architecture. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of manually applying domain-driven design to software systems by automating core activities through a prompting framework. The researchers built a framework that breaks down domain-driven design into five sequential steps and uses large language models to automate these steps. The result is a validated framework that can help streamline software design.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage software development teams, here is what to do: review your current design processes to see if they can be automated using this framework, assess the suitability of large language models for your specific needs, and consider integrating this framework into your development workflow.

case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of optimizing large language models (LLMs) for enterprise deployment, by building a framework called OptiKIT that automates model compression and tuning.
